prize_parts.citation: for measuring intergenerational mobility with population-scale administrative data and identifying the causal effects of place on children's outcomes

statement.case_for: My preferred ballot entry and names are unchanged from round 1. The criterion I weight most heavily across fields is measurement and causal identification done together. B002 meets it as well as any candidate. Linked population records make mobility a measurable, place-specific quantity. The movers and exposure-effect designs then test whether place causes outcomes, so the descriptive and causal strands can constrain each other. The work has changed research in public, labour and urban economics, and it has changed how opportunity is discussed in policy. What round 2 changed is how firmly I hold the details. The chair asked whether the three-name or the two-name version is preferable. I still prefer Chetty, Hendren and Friedman. The citation is about measurement with administrative data as well as causal place effects, and Friedman's role in the tax-record data work and the mobility studies fits the measurement half. A Chetty-Hendren pair would make the prize rest mainly on the causal strand, which is the part whose long-run robustness is still being tested. I would accept the pair as a fallback if the Committee judged Friedman's claim too diffuse. I have also narrowed the citation so that it does not assert a settled long-run causal verdict on neighbourhood effects. Katz stays off this part. His distinctive contributions are the Moving to Opportunity experiment and the skill-demand and wage-structure work, and both fit the framing of B038 better than this entry's framing around population-data measurement.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against my own first choice is the maturity asymmetry with B038. Core B002 results date from about 2014. The long-run causal neighbourhood estimates and their stability are still under test. The most influential evidence rests on restricted administrative data that outsiders cannot re-run. Credit sits inside one large collaborative group, so any three-name cap is arbitrary at the margin. Colleagues who rank B038 first can fairly argue that more than a decade of independent replication and critique has given its design a longer track record. The chair's question asks what evidence of long-run robustness I would need. I would want the exposure-effect and mover estimates to hold up in longer follow-up. I would also want register-based studies in other national settings to find patterns that are at least qualitatively similar. I have not verified that evidence here. If the Committee treats it as insufficient, the case for this year weakens, and I would lean to B038 with a citation limited to the trade-shock contribution.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first. In his file he is moved by Dreber's two-name version of B002 and says Friedman's case, which rests on data infrastructure and team contributions, is the weakest part of the attribution. He would back Chetty and Hendren over a three-name list if B002 were taken up.
responses.response: I take the attribution point seriously and would not call a Chetty-Hendren award indefensible. Our difference is what the citation is about. If the discovery is population-data measurement of mobility together with causal place effects, dropping Friedman narrows the prize to the causal strand, which is the less settled half and the one that raises most of the maturity concerns. Keeping him lets the measurement contribution, which is better established, carry some of the weight. I still treat the two-name version as the fallback if the Committee finds his individual claim too diffuse. I also accept your point about priority this year. It is a real comparison, and I have not changed my view that a result with a testable link to data should count for more than one whose validity is uncontested but empirically distant.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B038 first and B002 second. She presses on timing and verifiability: the mobility results mostly date from 2014 onward and depend on restricted administrative data, and the long-run causal reading of place effects is still being tested. She says she could support Chetty, Hendren and Friedman if the Committee prefers to reward the data-infrastructure advance.
responses.response: Your verifiability point is the objection I find hardest to answer, and I count it as a real discount on maturity rather than a footnote. My answer is partial. The causal claims that rest on movers and on re-analysis of a randomised experiment can be judged on the logic of the design, and the descriptive patterns can in principle be compared with register-based studies elsewhere. That is weaker than open-data replication, and I have not checked here how closely other settings agree. I am glad that your conditional support for the three-name list matches mine. My remaining difference with you is how much weight the longer replication history of B038 should get against the transparency of B002's measurement.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B038 first, having moved from Katz to Dorn. He separates the correlational mobility maps from the causal neighbourhood-effect estimates, ties Katz's role to the Moving to Opportunity experiment and to B038, and keeps B002 as an alternative because of timing.
responses.response: I agree with the descriptive/causal distinction and with leaving Katz out of the third slot here. That distinction also shapes how I read durability. The causal strand should carry the most weight in the citation, and its credit needs the most care. I do not accept that timing alone puts B002 below B038. Maturity and attribution are separate criteria. The B038 citation also has to be drafted narrowly to avoid claiming the task framework, and you accepted that in your own file. Both entries therefore need careful wording, and neither is clean. I read the maturity gap as a real difference of degree. It does not by itself settle the comparison.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B038 first. She argues that it has more than a decade of replication, critique and extension, whereas the neighbourhood-effect findings in B002 are still being tested for long-run robustness and for dependence on restricted data. She regards B002 as the natural alternative if the Committee judged it mature enough.
responses.response: The maturity asymmetry is correct, and it is why I describe B038 as my closest competitor and not a distant alternative. I would still ask that the comparison be symmetric. For B038 the open issues are the size and persistence of the China-shock effects, the shift-share debate and the Dorn-or-Katz choice. For B002 they are long-run robustness, restricted data and the Friedman-or-Katz choice. I am not equipped to settle the shift-share econometrics beyond what colleagues have said, so I give weight to your reading that the debate has refined the practice without overturning the core finding. I accept that your citation limited to trade and technology exposure and local adjustment is coherent. If the Committee wants the more seasoned empirical programme, I could support Autor, Hanson and Dorn with that narrow wording.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B012 first. He ranks B002 third and says the long-run causal verdict on neighbourhood effects is still developing and credit is spread across a large team. He is less confident than Dreber that this year is the right time, but would support Chetty, Hendren and Friedman if the Committee prefers it.
responses.response: I accept that the object of the prize is still developing, and I share your caution about team credit. On B012 I withdrew Gertler in round 1 and agree that Kiyotaki and Moore is the stronger two-person form. It remains my second choice. The mechanism is mature and foundational, but its direct empirical identification is mixed, as you and Strömberg both say, and that is why I rank it behind B002 on the evidence criterion. Our difference is how to weigh a mature mechanism with mixed identification against a younger programme with transparent measurement. I do not think support counts decide that. I am glad we agree on the three-name B002 list if it advances.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the mobility atlas (descriptive) and the causal place-effects work as one discovery, and how much of the citation's weight should fall on each.
Whether the third name should be Friedman, or whether the cleaner prize is the two-name Chetty-Hendren version. Katz has a real claim through Moving to Opportunity, but it overlaps B038.

Whether long-run follow-up and register-based studies in other settings will confirm the causal neighbourhood estimates. I have not verified this, and limited access to restricted data reduces independent checking.
Whether the maturity gap with B038 should decide the comparison, given that both entries have unresolved attribution questions.

How to compare conceptual mechanisms with mixed direct empirical tests (B012, B013, B001) against empirical programmes with debated magnitudes (B038, B002) without field familiarity deciding the comparison.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Chetty, Hendren, Friedman or Katz is apparent from the supplied profile. My profile lists a co-author named Persson on a corruption paper, without a first name, and B027 credits Torsten Persson. B027 is not in my configuration or alternatives, and I make no claim about the identity. My profile shows long-standing collaborations with Rothstein, Holmberg, Hadenius, Dahlström, Lapuente, Bäck, Lindvall and the V-Dem team, and none is credited on any shortlisted entry. I gave the 2024 presentation speech on institutions and prosperity. That speech reflects Academy drafting, does not show a preference among the 2026 candidates, and concerns different laureates. As a political scientist working on measurement and causal inference, I may favour B002 and B038, and I treat that as a field-familiarity disclosure rather than evidence of merit. Hassler, Krusell and Boppart are Stockholm University colleagues in a different department, and I weigh their arguments on the merits. I do not adjudicate any conflict.
